scores.notes: BUILT AND VERIFIED: g++ -std=c++11 -Wall -Wextra clean; 59/59 unit checks; test3/aaabd accepted in 11 steps, test3/aab rejected at step 6 via terminal mismatch, test1/(a,a) accepted in 12 steps -- every trace it prints matches its document verbatim, including the '出错：栈顶终结符“d”与当前输入符号“b”不匹配' string. FIDELITY (my lens): the ONLY design that supplies an explicit 'Clause map:' under all 12 items, mapping each phrase of each parser_*.yaml to the lines that satisfy it. Coverage is complete and the mappings are accurate, not decorative -- e.g. it is the only one to observe that part.substr(k+1) of a final occurrence is "", whose FIRST is {@}, so the yaml clauses 'use suffix FIRST sets when available' and 'recurse to parent FOLLOW sets at rule ends' collapse into one branch with no special-casing. Correctly keeps the 'recursive core' wording of parser_first_core/parser_follow_core (unlike robust). Q3 is the best-evidenced of the four: an exhaustive differential of textbook-FOLLOW vs seeded-FOLLOW over every string up to length 5 (3905/3905/1364 strings, 2 cell differences, 0 verdict differences) plus the correct accepted-language sets. Also independently found the real run_parser.sh 'cp x x' blocker (confirmed: exit 1 under set -e; since patched by maintainers exactly as suggested) and flagged the terminal.insert('#') caller-mutation. Honest about workspace drift. STYLE: left-aligned tables give the only genuinely readable grid of the four; the 步骤 column matches the Chinese-textbook trace layout the readme screenshots use; restores stream state with out << right. Slight deviation from the committed house style, but argued rather than accidental. CORRECTNESS DEDUCTIONS: shares the '#'-in-input false accept and the a@b bug (see criticalFlaws); its keep-first conflict policy produces a false REJECT on S::=Sa|b with input b, and it presents the step>1000 cap as merely 'terminating' without noting the verdict is wrong.

BUILT AND VERIFIED from commit 8a5ac40 (its listed code is byte-for-byte what got committed): -Wall -Wextra clean, 59/59 unit checks, all three traces exact. EVIDENCE QUALITY IS THE BEST OF THE FOUR: I checked its §4 'every line the program prints' transcript against the real binary and every single assertion holds -- 59 total lines, table rows exactly 68 bytes, trace rows exactly 60 bytes, line 35=23 bytes, 43=27, 44=21, 59=35, blank lines at 41/42/45/58. That level of measured precision is rare and it is all true. Also found the run_parser.sh 'cp x x' blocker (real; now patched). FIDELITY: covers all 12 requirements and every clause; the Q5 answer is the most precise of the four, and it is the only design that defends the setw/UTF-8 byte-padding choice with a direct citation (LexicalAnalysis.cpp:266 plus the intent of commit 5e4f0ee), rather than just asserting house style. Does not do explicit clause-by-clause mapping the way spec does, which is the only reason it does not edge ahead under my lens. CORRECTNESS DEDUCTIONS: on S::=b|S with input b (b IS in the language) it prints '字符串b不是该文法的句子' after dumping 10,035 lines -- wrong verdict plus a 10k-line spew, caused by last-write-wins conflicts colliding with the flat 10000-step cap. Also has the '#' false accept, the a@b bug, and is the only design that mutates the caller's terminal set (terminal.insert('#')), which it acknowledges in prose but keeps.

BUILT AND VERIFIED (fixpoint variant, with is_non_terminal deleted as it instructs): -Wall -Wextra clean, 59/59 unit checks, all three traces exact including its test3/'aa' spurious-[M,#] trace verbatim. I also verified its central claim that the fixpoint FIRST/FOLLOW output is byte-identical to the recursive version -- diffed the First/Follow report blocks across test1/test2/test3: identical on all three. BEST CORRECTNESS OF THE FOUR: it is the ONLY design that handles '@' occurring inside a longer right part (per-character 'if (right_part[k] == '@') continue;' instead of 'if (right != "@")'). On S::=a@b|c with input ab it is the only one that correctly accepts. This is not hypothetical -- the maintainers landed exactly this fix in commit e7384b5 while I was judging. Its fixpoint is also provably terminating rather than heuristically guarded, and its step cap is proportional (500+100n), which the maintainers also converged on. It is also the only design honest about the conflict-policy trade-off, correctly predicting that keep-first and last-wins each get lucky on mirrored grammars -- confirmed: keep-first rejects S::=Sa|b/b, last-wins rejects S::=b|S/b. FIDELITY DEDUCTION (my lens): its headline recommendation replaces recursion with iteration, which contradicts the literal wording of two requirements -- parser_first_core.yaml says 'the RECURSIVE core of FIRST-set computation' and parser_follow_core.yaml says 'RECURSE to parent FOLLOW sets at rule ends'. It hedges that the recursive version is 'defensible', but under a clause-coverage lens the primary proposal under-satisfies 2 of 12. It also missed the run_parser.sh blocker, and its own advertised unknown-symbol pre-check has a hole it never noticed: find_col(table,'#') succeeds because '#' is a column, so '#' sails straight through. STYLE: house-conforming, but the parallel-vector fixpoint machinery reads less like the rest of this lab file, and it prints a 警告 conflict line from inside LL_1, injecting noise into the report section.

BUILT AND VERIFIED: -Wall -Wextra clean, 59/59 unit checks, and all three hand traces reproduce exactly as documented (aaabd accepted in 11 steps, aab rejected at step 6, (a,a) accepted in 12 steps, plus the '出错：分析栈顶的“d”与当前输入符号“b”无法匹配' line verbatim). Its Q1-Q6 reasoning is sound throughout: the Q3 safety argument is the cleanest of the four, and it is the only one to notice the asymmetry that in test1 the spurious '#' in Follow(T) never reaches the grid because T has no nullable candidate, while Follow(G)'s does. Correctly keeps the recursive core the yaml asks for, avoids mutating the caller's terminal set, and shares the same correct row/col/indexing/start-symbol answers as the others. FIDELITY: all 12 requirements covered with all clauses satisfied; less explicit clause-by-clause mapping than spec, and it missed the run_parser.sh 'cp x x' blocker that formats and spec both caught. CORRECTNESS -- WORST RUNTIME FAILURE OF THE FOUR: the delivered parse loop has no step cap, so a cyclic table entry spins forever. On grammar S::=b|S with input b it did not terminate within 10 seconds, having emitted 2,652,810 trace lines. It does disclose this and supplies the fix, but explicitly labels it 'Optional hardening, not required by the lab' and leaves it out of the delivered code, so the artifact as handed over hangs. Also shares the '#' false accept and the a@b bug. STYLE: house-conforming tabs/Chinese comments/setw, but its setw(6)+setw(16)x3 trace header is the most visually mangled of the four -- setw(16) barely exceeds the 15-byte Chinese labels, so the header collapses to '步骤       分析栈 剩余输入串 所用产生式' with essentially no column structure.

criticalFlaws: ALL FOUR DESIGNS -- '#' in the input string is treated as a legitimate grammar symbol, producing a false ACCEPT. Concrete input: grammar test2 (E::=AB|a A::=C|bDA B::=@ C::=cAD|@ D::=dBe), input string '#'. All four binaries print '字符串#是该文法的句子'. '#' is not a terminal of test2, so the string '#' cannot be a sentence. Cause: the input char '#' is pushed onto the input stack above the '#' sentinel; since epsilon is in L(test2) the analysis stack drains to '#' while the lookahead is the input's own '#', and the 'top==# && cur==#' accept test fires. Note robust's own unknown-symbol pre-check does NOT catch this, because find_col(table,'#') succeeds ('#' is the last column). The maintainers independently identified and fixed this during my review (commit e7384b5, adding 'if (input.find('#') != string::npos)').

ALL EXCEPT robust (faithful, formats, spec) -- an '@' appearing INSIDE a longer right part is pushed onto the analysis stack as a literal symbol instead of being treated as epsilon, causing a false REJECT. Concrete input: grammar 'S::=a@b|c', input 'ab'. faithful/formats/spec all print '字符串ab不是该文法的句子'; robust correctly prints '是该文法的句子'. Cause: 'if (right != "@") { push every char }' only skips a candidate that is exactly "@", whereas robust does the per-character 'if (right_part[k] == '@') continue;'. The maintainers shipped robust's exact formulation in commit e7384b5.

faithful ONLY -- the delivered parse loop contains no step cap, so a cyclic LL(1)-table entry makes syntacticAnalysis loop forever and emit unbounded output. Concrete input: grammar 'S::=b|S', input 'b'. The binary did not terminate within a 10-second timeout, having written 2,652,810 trace lines to stdout. faithful's own last-write-wins builder puts M[S,b] = S::=S, so the loop pops S and pushes S indefinitely. The design predicts this exact scenario and supplies the guard, but files it under 'Optional hardening, not required by the lab' and omits it from the delivered code.

formats -- last-write-wins conflict resolution combined with a flat 10,000-step cap yields a wrong verdict plus a 10k-line output dump on a string that is in the language. Concrete input: grammar 'S::=b|S', input 'b' (b IS in L, since S ::= b). Output: '字符串b不是该文法的句子' after 10,035 lines. The candidate 'S' is written to M[S,b] after the candidate 'b', overwriting the only usable entry.

robust AND spec -- keep-first conflict resolution produces a false REJECT on strings that are in the language, on the mirrored grammar. Concrete inputs: grammar 'S::=Sa|b', input 'b' -> both print '字符串b不是该文法的句子' (robust after 636 lines, spec after 1036); grammar 'S::=A  A::=S|b', input 'b' -> same wrong verdict from both. robust documents this trade-off explicitly and correctly; spec does not -- it claims only that the step>1000 cap makes the run 'terminate', without noting the verdict it terminates with is wrong.

robust -- assembly hazard that will not compile if the document is followed literally. Item 7 leaves the body of LL_1() open with the comment '/* …builder half follows… */', and item 8 then begins with a new 'static void fill_cell(LL_1_table&, const int, const char, const rule)' function definition before resuming the LL_1() body with '/* …continues LL_1() … */'. Pasted in the given order this places a function definition inside another function body, which is illegal C++ ('error: a function-definition is not allowed here before '{' token', verified with g++). fill_cell must be hoisted above LL_1.

formats -- LL_1 mutates its caller's set through a non-const reference via 'terminal.insert('#')'. Latent rather than currently observable: it is safe only because main() happens to call check_set(terminal, ...) before LL_1(...). Any reordering of main(), a second LL_1 call, or a unit test that re-inspects the terminal set after building the table would see a phantom '#' terminal. faithful, robust and spec all avoid this by filtering '#'/'@' on the way out and appending '#' to col directly; formats notes the hazard in prose but keeps the mutation.

scores.notes: VERIFIED: spliced into the baseline (/tmp/j3/robust.cpp) -> g++ -std=c++11 -Wall -Wextra -Wshadow clean, 59/59 unit checks, all three required traces byte-identical to its quoted output. Strongest under my lens for three provable reasons. (1) ONLY design that predicts a concrete -Wall diagnostic: I re-added is_non_terminal to its fixpoint build and got exactly "warning: 'bool is_non_terminal(char, const std::vector<rule>&)' defined but not used [-Wunused-function]". Verbatim match. (2) Its exponential-blowup claim is real and its numbers honest: 20-non-terminal chain grammar -> faithful 3.41s, formats 3.47s, spec 9.01s, robust 0.02s. Only design whose FIRST/FOLLOW is polynomial. (3) Only design that both terminates AND gives the correct verdict on cyclic S::=a|S with input 'a' (39 lines, ACCEPT). It also correctly diagnoses the terminal.insert('#') aliasing side effect in the other designs and removes it. Its self-reported keep-first weakness is real and honestly stated: S::=Sa|b input 'b' rejects a genuine sentence (637 lines to the cap); it says outright neither conflict policy is systematically safer, which my testing confirms. Deductions: item-8 presentation is a literal compile error (see criticalFlaws); recomputes allFirst/allFollow from scratch on every findFirst/findFollow call; its out-of-grammar pre-check emits a trace header with zero rows, which looks broken; 3 -Wconversion warnings (benign size_type->unsigned int index math, most of the four).

VERIFIED: splices verbatim, -Wall -Wextra -Wshadow clean, 59/59, traces exact. Best documentation by a wide margin - its annotated 59-line full-output listing is structurally exact: I measured 59 total lines, table rows 68 bytes, trace rows 60 bytes, verdict 35 bytes, all matching. (A few Chinese-heavy header lines are off by 1-3 bytes, apparently counting the fullwidth colon as 2 rather than 3, but every load-bearing number is right.) Its ostringstream-before-setw explanation and its UTF-8/setw analysis citing LexicalAnalysis.cpp:266 are correct. It also caught a real harness bug (run_parser.sh doing cp test3.txt test3.txt, aborting under set -e); the tree has since been patched with exactly the guard it proposed. Deductions: knowingly ships terminal.insert('#') in LL_1, mutating the caller's set through a non-const reference and dead besides; last-write-wins on conflicts with no warning; on the cyclic grammar it emits 10,036 lines then the WRONG verdict; hoists rule rule_temp outside the parse loop and mutates it in place, so the action column is correct only because every branch remembers to clear right. Shares the unmentioned exponential FIRST/FOLLOW.

VERIFIED: splices verbatim, -Wall/-Wextra/-Wshadow clean, 59/59, traces exact, and cleanest of the four at -Wconversion (0 vs 1/2/3) because it never narrows size_type to unsigned int. Best fidelity argument: only design that quotes each requirement yaml clause and maps it to the lines implementing it, which matches how those yamls are actually written (I read all of them). Its differential experiment (spurious-# vs textbook FOLLOW over 3905/3905/1364 strings, 0 verdict differences) is real - my own exhaustive run over all strings up to length 4 on all three grammars found zero verdict differences between all four designs, and its length-5 accepted sets for test1 (10 strings, exact list) and test3 ({ad,aad,aaabd,aaebd}) match mine exactly. Keep-first means it terminates AND is correct on S::=a|S. Its index-scan for repeated non-terminals in one candidate is the cleanest of the four. Deductions: SLOWEST design (9.01s on the 20-NT chain, 3x worse than faithful/formats) because its builder calls findFollow(rules[i].left, rules) once per rule unconditionally, hoisted outside the candidate loop, paying FOLLOW cost even for grammars with no epsilon; deviates from house style with left/right stream manipulators where LexicalAnalysis.cpp:266 uses bare right-aligned setw (its grid is the most readable, so defensible, but the brief said copy the sibling); reports test2's accepted set as 3 when it is 4 (omits the empty string its own code correctly accepts); shares the undisclosed keep-first mis-verdict on S::=Sa|b.

VERIFIED: the most drop-in-clean design - splices verbatim with zero edits, -Wall -Wextra -Wshadow clean, 59/59, and its three required traces (test3/aaabd 11 rows, test3/aab terminal-mismatch at #d vs b, test1/(a,a) 12 rows) reproduce byte-for-byte. Style is the closest match to LexicalAnalysis.cpp of the four (bare right-aligned setw, no manipulators, tabs, correct Chinese comment register). Q1-Q6 answers all correct; the Q3 safety argument for unconditional '#' seeding is sound - I confirmed the spurious [G,#] cell fires on test1 input '(a' and the string is still rejected. But it carries the ONLY catastrophic runtime failure of the four (see criticalFlaws): no step cap, so a cyclic grammar hangs with unbounded output, and it relegates the fix to 'Optional hardening, not required by the lab' - the wrong call, since a hang is strictly worse for a harness than a wrong verdict. Also shares the exponential FIRST/FOLLOW (3.41s on the 20-NT chain) and hand-waves it as 'microseconds' without measuring; and the '(a' trace it presents as a literal program capture shows step numbers 9 and 10 when the real run produces 6 and 7 - content right, but that block is not the output it is presented as. string right = cell.right[0] shadows std::right; harmless here and flagged by neither -Wall nor -Wshadow, but a latent trap.

criticalFlaws: faithful - INFINITE LOOP with unbounded output. Grammar `S::=a|S`, input `a`. Last-write-wins cell assignment puts S::=S into [S,a]; the parse loop has no step cap (faithful offers one only as 'Optional hardening, not required by the lab'). Measured: exit code 124 under `timeout 5`, 1,251,297 trace lines / 69,071,322 bytes in 5 seconds. The only design of the four that can hang a harness rather than merely answer wrongly, and no compiler diagnostic can catch it.

robust - HARD COMPILE ERROR as literally presented. Item 7 (parser_ll1_header) ends mid-function with `/* ...builder half follows... */` still inside LL_1(), and item 8 opens with `static void fill_cell(LL_1_table&, const int, const char, const rule) { ... }` followed by `/* ...continues LL_1() ... */`. Spliced literally that nests a free function definition inside LL_1(). Minimal repro confirmed: g++ -std=c++11 -Wall gives `error: a function-definition is not allowed here before '{' token`. Fixed by hoisting fill_cell above LL_1; with that single move the design compiles clean under -Wall -Wextra -Wshadow and passes 59/59.

formats - WRONG VERDICT on a cyclic grammar. Grammar `S::=a|S`, input `a` (which IS a sentence). Last-write-wins puts S::=S in [S,a]; the 10000-step cap then fires, printing 10,036 lines before concluding 'a is NOT a sentence'. Terminates, but noisy and incorrect. robust and spec get this right via keep-first.

robust and spec - WRONG VERDICT from keep-first conflict policy. Grammar `S::=Sa|b`, input `b` (which IS a sentence). Keep-first parks the left-recursive S::=Sa in [S,b]; the parse spins to the step cap and rejects - robust at 637 lines, spec at 1037 lines. faithful and formats accept by luck of last-write-wins. robust states this trade-off explicitly and correctly; spec does not mention it.

faithful, formats, spec - EXPONENTIAL FIRST/FOLLOW, measured. On a 20-non-terminal re-converging chain (A::=xB|yB  B::=xC|yC ... T::=z, input z): faithful 3.41s, formats 3.47s, spec 9.01s, robust 0.02s. The DFS `visiting` guard blocks back-edges but re-explores cross-edges. Only robust's fixpoint eliminates it. spec is worst because its builder calls findFollow(rules[i].left, rules) once per rule unconditionally, outside the candidate loop, so it pays FOLLOW cost even on grammars with no epsilon-production.

formats - `terminal.insert('#')` inside `LL_1(set<char>& terminal, ...)` mutates the caller's set through a non-const reference. It is also dead code: the following loop filters '#' out and then push_back('#') runs unconditionally, so it changes nothing about the output. Not observable in the current main() only because check_set(terminal, ...) runs before LL_1; it breaks the moment anyone reorders main() or calls LL_1 twice. robust and spec both identify this and remove it; formats acknowledges it and ships it anyway.

scores.notes: Best measured parse-correctness: 59/59 units, 34/36 e2e, terminates on every pathological grammar I threw at it (exit 0 with the 10000-step cap). Last-write-wins conflict policy is the one that happens to satisfy both shipped pathological cases (S::=Sa|b + 'b', A::=B B::=A|c + 'c'). Two real defects: the '@'-inside-a-right-part bug (A::=a@b + 'ab' wrongly rejected) and the shared 'ad#' false accept. Q5 is far and away the best answer of the four -- a full 59-line output map with provenance per line, and I confirmed the load-bearing structural claims (59 lines total, 68-byte table rows, 60-byte trace rows, blank-line positions, trailing-space columns) are all exactly right. Two doc errors in that same section: it claims all three test*.txt end in a newline (none do -- last bytes are '@', ' ', 'e'), and roughly eight of its per-line byte counts are undercounted (line 1 is 38 not 34, line 20 is 29 not 26, line 29 is 30 not 28). Correctly reported the run_parser.sh 'cp x x' abort. Style is house style exactly: default-right setw, tabs, Chinese comments, ostringstream-before-setw explained. Note this design is effectively the code already committed at HEAD, so it adds little novelty -- but through a parse-correctness lens it measures best.

Ties formats on the e2e count (34/36) but has a strictly worse failure mode: it does not terminate. It deliberately relegates the loop cap to 'Optional hardening, not required by the lab', so grammar S::=b|Sa with input 'b' runs until killed (exit 124 after 30 s), emitting trace rows without bound while the analysis stack grows one symbol per step. S::=b|S does the same. Every other design terminates on both. Its own reasoning ('None of test1/test2/test3 can reach this') is true but the repo has a dedicated pathological-grammar test class. Also carries the '@'-in-middle bug and the 'ad#' false accept. Q3 proof is the cleanest prose argument of the four and its reachability analysis of the spurious [G,#] cell is correct. Verification-integrity ding: the 'real run' excerpt for test1 input '(a' is labelled steps 9 and 10; the actual steps are 6 and 7 -- the format is exact, the numbers are not. It also lists 'run_parser.sh test3.txt aaabd' among its test invocations, which aborted before the build in the state it was written against.

The best engineering, the wrong recommendation. It is the ONLY design that skips '@' char-by-char when pushing the RHS, so it alone passes A::=a@b + 'ab' -- and HEAD has since adopted exactly that fix, vindicating the call. Its fixpoint FIRST/FOLLOW is genuinely correct and I measured 0.017 s vs 3.2-3.4 s for the guarded-recursion designs on the 20-non-terminal chain, so the exponential diagnosis is real. But it recommends keep-first conflict resolution, which regresses two cases the repo explicitly tests (S::=Sa|b + 'b' and A::=B B::=A|c + 'c' both flip to rejected), dropping it to 33/36. To its credit it is the only design that correctly states the symmetry -- reversing to S::=b|Sa flips which policy wins -- and I confirmed that empirically; it just picked the side that loses the shipped tests. Also carries the 'ad#' false accept: its unknown-symbol pre-check cannot catch it because '#' is a legitimate column. Fidelity ding: parser_first_core says 'the recursive core' and parser_follow_core says 'recurse to parent FOLLOW sets', and its recommended code removes recursion entirely (it does offer the recursive variant as option (a)). Its MAX_STEP of 500+100*|w| is much tighter than the others; I could not construct a realistic false-reject but the margin is thin. Correctly flagged the terminal.insert('#') aliasing and verified no conflict warning fires on the three shipped grammars (I confirmed: 0, 0, 0).

Worst measured parse-correctness of the four: 32/36. It stacks both discriminating defects -- keep-first (loses S::=Sa|b + 'b' and A::=B B::=A|c + 'c') AND the '@'-in-middle bug (loses A::=a@b + 'ab') -- plus the shared 'ad#' false accept. Its own claim that 'the lab's grammars never hit' the conflict path is falsified by two cases already in test_parser_e2e.sh. Also the slowest by a wide margin at 6.81 s on the 20-NT chain, roughly 2x the other recursive designs, because it hoists findFollow(rules[i].left) outside the candidate loop and pays for FOLLOW on every rule whether or not any candidate is nullable. Style: 'cout << left' deviates from the sibling lexer, which uses default-right setw at LexicalAnalysis.cpp:268 and :274 -- more readable output, but the brief asked to copy that file's style. Genuine strengths that keep fidelity high: the per-clause requirement mapping is the most rigorous of the four (it walks each yaml phrase to the line that implements it), the Q3 evidence is the strongest offered by anyone (a brute-force differential over every string up to length 5 against a textbook-FOLLOW build, 0 verdict differences), and it correctly reported the run_parser.sh 'cp x x' abort and the terminal.insert('#') aliasing.

criticalFlaws: SHARED BY ALL FOUR -- false ACCEPT of a non-sentence. Grammar test3 (E::=aH H::=aMd|d M::=Ab|@ A::=aM|e), input 'ad#'. All four print 字符串ad#是该文法的句子. '#' is pushed as an ordinary input character, so after E::=aH / match a / H::=d / match d the analysis stack is '#' and the input top is the USER's '#', and the top=='#' && cur=='#' accept branch fires. This is the most severe class of parser bug (accepting a string outside the language) and no design mentions it. Robust's unknown-symbol pre-check does not catch it because '#' is a legitimate column. HEAD has since fixed it with an explicit input.find('#') guard.

faithful -- NON-TERMINATION with unbounded memory growth. Grammar 'S::=b|Sa', input 'b'. Measured exit=124 (killed) after 30 s; also 'S::=b|S' + 'b', exit=124. The design places the step cap under 'Optional hardening, not required by the lab', so the parse loop has no bound. With last-write-wins, [S,b] holds S::=Sa; each iteration pops S and pushes 'a','S', so the analysis stack grows by one symbol per step forever while print_state emits a row (and rebuilds the whole growing string) each time. Every other design terminates on both grammars. formats, with the same conflict policy, terminates at exit 0 via its 10000-step cap.

faithful and formats and spec -- '@' inside a right part is pushed onto the analysis stack. The guard is the whole-string test if (right != "@"). Grammar 'A::=a@b', input 'ab'. All three print 字符串ab不是该文法的句子; correct is 是. Trace: [A,a]=A::=a@b, push reverse -> stack #b@a, match 'a', then stack top '@' is not a row header so it is treated as a terminal and compared against lookahead 'b' -> mismatch. Robust is the only design that gets this right (it skips '@' character-by-character), and HEAD has since adopted robust's fix.

robust and spec -- keep-first conflict resolution regresses two acceptance cases the repo explicitly tests. robust's fill_cell and spec's occupancy check both refuse to overwrite an occupied cell. Grammar 'S::=Sa|b', input 'b' -> both print 字符串b不是该文法的句子 (correct: 是); grammar 'A::=B  B::=A|c', input 'c' -> both print 字符串c不是该文法的句子 (correct: 是). Both are named cases in /workspace/agent_tests/test_parser_e2e.sh under the comment 病态文法不能让分析器崩溃或者死循环. In both, keep-first parks the self-referential production (S::=Sa, B::=A) in the cell and the parse spins until the step cap trips. I verified by patching only this one policy into an otherwise-passing build: 28 cases, exactly 2 failures, both of these.

spec -- worst aggregate parse-correctness: it is the only design carrying BOTH the keep-first regression and the '@'-in-middle bug, so it fails 4 of 36 e2e cases (S::=Sa|b + 'b', A::=B B::=A|c + 'c', A::=a@b + 'ab', test3 + 'ad#'), against 2 for formats and faithful and 3 for robust.
